## Scope

This document specifies the mathematics of the model as **implemented in this
package**, not the mathematics of GLM-HMMs in general. Where the code makes an
assumption or an approximation, it is flagged inline as:

> **[A]** an *assumption* — something taken to be true about the data or the
> model, which the code does not check.
>
> **[X]** an *approximation* — a quantity the code replaces with something
> cheaper, incurring an error.

The short answer to "is the model selection code an approximation?" is: **yes, at
several independent levels**, and the factorized evidence estimators (BQ and SMC)
are approximations of an approximation. @sec-summary tabulates every one.

Notation: $K$ hidden states, $S$ independent sequences, sequence $i$ of length
$T_i$. Superscripts for sequence index are dropped where unambiguous.

---

## The generative model

### Latent chain

A discrete-state Markov chain $z_{1:T}$, $z_t \in \{1,\dots,K\}$:

$$
z_1 \sim \mathrm{Cat}(\pi_0), \qquad
z_{t+1} \mid z_t = i \;\sim\; \mathrm{Cat}\big(A_t[i,\cdot]\big).
$$

The package stores $\log \pi_0$ directly. Transitions come in two forms.

**Static.** A single row-stochastic $A \in \mathbb{R}^{K\times K}$, stored as
$\log A$.

**Input-driven.** Given transition covariates $u_t \in \mathbb{R}^{D_u}$ and
parameters $\theta \in \mathbb{R}^{D_u \times K \times K}$,

$$
A_t[i,j] \;=\; \frac{\exp\big(u_t^\top \theta[:,i,j]\big)}
                    {\sum_{j'} \exp\big(u_t^\top \theta[:,i,j']\big)} .
$$

Each source state $i$ has its own multinomial logistic regression over
destinations. For identifiability the last destination is the reference
category, $\theta[:,i,K] = 0$; the M-step enforces this exactly.

> **[A] Transition input alignment.** $u_t$ indexes the *transition* $t \to
> t+1$, so $u$ has length $T-1$ for a sequence of $T$ observations. This is
> checked by `_validate_data_shapes` at fit time. Downstream entry points
> (`compute_log_marginal_likelihood`, `viterbi`) do **not** re-check it.

Which form is used is decided by whether `data.x_trans` is present — there is no
separate flag.

### Emissions

Given $z_t = k$, the observation at $t$ may consist of several modalities. The
package supports five families; any subset may be active simultaneously.

Let $x_t^{f}$ be the covariates for family $f$ and $W^f_{:,k}$ its weights for
state $k$. With $\sigma(\cdot)$ the logistic function:

| Family | Density | Link | Extra parameter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli | $y^{\,y}(1-y)^{1-y}$, $p = \sigma(x^\top w_k)$ | logit | — |
| Multinomial | $\mathrm{Cat}\big(\mathrm{softmax}(x^\top W_k)\big)$ | softmax | — |
| Neg. binomial | $\mathrm{NB}(\mu_k, \phi_k)$, $\mu_k = e^{x^\top w_k}$ | log | dispersion $\phi_k$ |
| Gamma | $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_k, \beta_k)$, $\beta_k = \alpha_k/\mu_k$, $\mu_k = e^{x^\top w_k}$ | log | shape $\alpha_k$ |
| Gaussian | $\mathcal{N}(x^\top W_k, \Sigma_k)$, $y \in \mathbb{R}^M$ | identity | covariance $\Sigma_k$ |

Explicitly, the negative binomial is parameterized by mean and dispersion,

$$
\log p(y \mid \mu, \phi) = \log\Gamma(y+\phi) - \log\Gamma(y+1) - \log\Gamma(\phi)
 + \phi \log\!\frac{\phi}{\phi+\mu} + y \log\!\frac{\mu}{\phi+\mu},
$$

and the Gamma uses a mean parameterization with state-specific shape,

$$
\log p(y \mid \alpha, \mu) = \alpha\log\beta - \log\Gamma(\alpha)
 + (\alpha-1)\log y - \beta y, \qquad \beta = \alpha/\mu .
$$

Multinomial weights use the last category as reference, $W^{\text{mn}}[:,C,:] = 0$.

> **[A] Conditional independence across families.** Given $z_t$, the active
> modalities are independent, so their log-likelihoods **add**:
> $$\log p(y_t \mid z_t=k) = \sum_f \log p_f\big(y_t^f \mid x_t^f, W^f_{:,k}\big).$$
> This is what `compute_total_emissions` computes. Any residual correlation
> between, say, choice and neural activity beyond what the shared state explains
> is not modelled.

> **[A] Numerical guards change the model in the tails.** Log-link means are
> clipped: $\log\mu \le 20$ (neg. binomial) and $\log\mu \in [-10, 20]$ (Gamma).
> Inside the clipped region the gradient is exactly zero, so a state whose fitted
> rate saturates will stop moving rather than diverge.

### Gaussian data at a different sampling rate {#sec-gauss-rate}

Gaussian observations may arrive faster than the latent chain evolves — e.g.
many neural samples per behavioural trial. Sample $s$ belongs to HMM step $t$,
given by index arrays `gauss_first_idx` / `gauss_last_idx`, so that step $t$ owns
samples $[\,\mathrm{first}_t,\ \mathrm{last}_t)$ of length $L_t$.

The step-level contribution is the **sum** over its segment:

$$
\ell^{\text{gauss}}_t(k) \;=\; \sum_{s \in \text{seg}(t)}
   \log \mathcal{N}\big(y_s \mid x_s^\top W_k,\ \Sigma_k\big).
$$

> **[A] Segments are contiguous, in order, and tile the array from index 0.**
> The implementation builds segment identifiers from the segment *lengths*
> (`repeat(arange(n_seg), last - first)`) and never uses the *positions*
> `first`/`last` themselves. Contiguous ordered segments — the documented layout
> — are handled correctly. Segments supplied out of order are silently
> mis-assigned; segments with gaps make the lengths fail to sum to $N$ and raise.
> **It is the caller's responsibility to supply ordered, contiguous indices.**

### The Gaussian rescaling heuristic {#sec-gauss-norm}

> **[X] Pseudo-likelihood reweighting.** When Gaussian data is fit *alongside*
> another family, each segment's summed log-likelihood is divided by its length
> and by the number of channels $M$:
> $$
> \tilde{\ell}^{\text{gauss}}_t(k) = \frac{1}{L_t\,M}\sum_{s \in \text{seg}(t)}
> \log \mathcal{N}\big(y_s \mid x_s^\top W_k, \Sigma_k\big).
> $$
> This stops $L_t M$ neural terms from swamping a single binary choice. It is
> **not** a likelihood: with it active, everything downstream — the "LML", BIC,
> CV scores, and the evidence estimates — is a pseudo-likelihood quantity.
> Values are comparable to each other but not to an unrescaled fit.
>
> Controlled by `GLMHMMConfig.normalize_gauss_loglik`; `None` (default) enables
> it exactly when another family is present. It applies to the E-step, the
> forward pass, Viterbi and both evidence estimators, but **not** to the Gaussian
> M-step, which remains a responsibility-weighted ridge on the raw samples. The
> weight $1/(L_t M)$ is fixed; there is no tunable modality-balance parameter.

### Joint density

$$
p(y_{1:T}, z_{1:T} \mid \Theta) = \pi_0[z_1]\;
\prod_{t=1}^{T-1} A_t[z_t, z_{t+1}] \;
\prod_{t=1}^{T} \prod_f p_f\big(y^f_t \mid x^f_t, W^f_{:,z_t}\big),
$$

with $\Theta = \{\pi_0,\ \theta \text{ or } A,\ W^f,\ \phi,\ \alpha,\ \Sigma\}$.
Sequences are assumed independent, so log-likelihoods add across them.

---

## Inference

### Forward–backward

Both passes run in log space with per-step normalization. With
$\ell_t(k) = \log p(y_t \mid z_t = k)$:

$$
\log\alpha_1 = \ell_1 + \log\pi_0 - c_1, \qquad
\log\alpha_t = \ell_t + \log\!\!\sum_i \exp\big(\log A_{t-1}[i,\cdot] + \log\alpha_{t-1}[i]\big) - c_t,
$$

where $c_t$ is the log normalizer of the bracket, so each $\alpha_t$ sums to 1.
The **exact** log marginal likelihood is then

$$
\log p(y_{1:T}\mid\Theta) = \sum_{t=1}^{T} c_t .
$$

The backward pass uses the same scaling constants, and

$$
\gamma_t(k) = \frac{\alpha_t(k)\beta_t(k)}{\sum_{k'}\alpha_t(k')\beta_t(k')}, \qquad
\xi_t(i,j) = \alpha_t(i)\,A_t[i,j]\,p(y_{t+1}\mid j)\,\beta_{t+1}(j)\,e^{-c_{t+1}} .
$$

There are **no approximations here**: these are exact given $\Theta$, and the
implementation was verified against exhaustive enumeration of all $K^T$ paths
(agreement to $\sim10^{-16}$), including the marginalization identities
$\sum_j \xi_t(i,j) = \gamma_t(i)$ and $\sum_i \xi_t(i,j) = \gamma_{t+1}(j)$.

### Viterbi

Exact max-product recursion with backtracking; verified against exhaustive
argmax over all paths. Note this returns the single most likely *path*, which is
generally not the sequence of per-step marginal modes $\arg\max_k \gamma_t(k)$.

---

## Learning: MAP-EM

### Objective

The package does **not** compute a maximum-likelihood fit. The L2 penalties are
Gaussian priors, so `fit_glmhmm` performs MAP-EM, ascending

$$
\mathcal{F}(\Theta) \;=\; \log p(Y \mid \Theta) \;+\; \log p(\Theta),
$$

with the implied prior, per emission family and per state,

$$
w_0 \sim \mathcal{N}\!\big(0,\ \texttt{prior\_var\_bias\_emit}\big), \qquad
w_{d>0} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\big(0,\ 1/\texttt{l2\_reg\_}f\big),
$$

and the analogous pair (`prior_var_bias_trans`, `l2_reg_trans`) for $\theta$.
**Column 0 of every design matrix is assumed to be the bias.** This convention is
load-bearing: the evidence code reconstructs "which entries are bias" from
flattened index arithmetic.

The Gaussian family is the exception to the isotropic form above. Its closed-form
M-step implies a *matrix-normal* prior whose column covariance is the noise
covariance itself,
$W_k \mid \Sigma_k \sim \mathcal{MN}(0, \Lambda^{-1}, \Sigma_k)$ with
$\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\rho)$,
$\rho_0 = 1/\texttt{prior\_var\_bias\_emit}$ and
$\rho_{d>0} = \texttt{l2\_reg\_gauss}$. @sec-gauss-exact uses exactly this prior,
so the fit and the evidence describe the same model.

The initial-state update uses a $\mathrm{Dir}(1.0001)$ prior (essentially flat,
for numerical safety).

### EM {#sec-em}

**E-step** — exact posteriors $\gamma, \xi$ from forward–backward, as above.

**M-step** — maximize $\mathbb{E}_q[\log p(Y,Z\mid\Theta)] + \log p(\Theta)$.
Because the complete-data likelihood factorizes, this splits into independent
problems:

- **$\pi_0$**: closed form, $\pi_0 \propto \sum_i \gamma^{(i)}_1 + (\text{Dir. pseudo-counts})$.
- **Static $A$**: closed form, $A[i,j] \propto \sum_t \xi_t(i,j)$, plus
  `transition_stickiness` added to the diagonal as a pseudo-count.
- **Input-driven $\theta$**: for each source state $i$ independently, a
  responsibility-weighted multinomial logistic regression solved by L-BFGS,
  $$
  \min_{\theta_i} \; -\sum_t \sum_j \xi_t(i,j)\,\log A_t[i,j] \;+\; \text{penalty}.
  $$
- **Bernoulli / multinomial / neg. binomial / Gamma**: per state, a
  $\gamma$-weighted GLM fit by L-BFGS. Dispersion parameters $\phi,\alpha$ are
  optimized jointly with the weights in log space.
- **Gaussian**: closed form. $W_k$ solves the weighted ridge system
  $(X^\top\Gamma_k X + \Lambda)W_k = X^\top\Gamma_k Y$, with
  $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\rho)$ as above -- the bias row is penalised like every
  other family's, not left free -- and
  $\Sigma_k = \sum_n \gamma_{nk} r_n r_n^\top / \sum_n \gamma_{nk} + \epsilon I$
  with $\epsilon = 10^{-3}$.

Each of these was verified to (i) equal $-\sum_n \gamma_{nk}\log p(y_n\mid\cdot)
+ \text{penalty}$ exactly, and (ii) return a stationary point of that objective.
The whole loop was verified to increase $\mathcal{F}$ monotonically.

> **[X] Numerical M-step tolerances.** The GLM M-steps are iterative (L-BFGS,
> default `tol=1e-3`), not exact maximizations — this is generalized EM.
> Monotonicity of $\mathcal{F}$ still holds provided each M-step improves its
> objective.

> **[X] The returned parameters lag their own responsibilities.** $\Theta_{t+1}$
> maximizes an objective built from the E-step at $\Theta_t$. At a true fixed
> point the two coincide, but EM stops on a *log-likelihood* tolerance, so in
> practice the returned $\hat\Theta$ is not a stationary point of the objective
> rebuilt from a fresh E-step at $\hat\Theta$. Measured on a $K=4$ fit of a true
> $K=3$ model, the gradient norms of the four transition factors at $\hat\Theta$
> were $0.23$, $1.37$, $2.23$ and $0.34$ — not $\sim 10^{-10}$ as they are for a
> single M-step in isolation. This is the assumption the Laplace step in
> @sec-factorized depends on, and it is only approximately met. Tighten `tol` and
> raise `num_em_iters` before trusting a Laplace-based evidence.

> **[X] Dispersion epsilon.** The neg. binomial and Gamma objectives optimize
> with $\phi + 10^{-6}$ (resp. $\alpha + 10^{-6}$) but *return* $\phi$ without
> it, so the E-step scores a parameter $10^{-6}$ away from the one the M-step
> optimized. The Gamma objective additionally mixes the two: its shape uses
> $\alpha+10^{-6}$ while its rate is built from $\alpha$, so it is not exactly a
> Gamma density for any single $\alpha$ (implied mean $\mu(1+10^{-6}/\alpha)$).
> Relative effect $\sim 10^{-7}$; it floors the attainable gradient norm for
> these two families at $\sim10^{-4}$. This is now the *only* precision floor in
> the objectives: the observations previously carried a hardcoded
> `astype(float32)` and now follow the dtype of the computation, so
> `jax_enable_x64` is honoured end to end.

> **[A] Local optima.** EM converges to a local optimum of a non-convex
> objective. `fit_with_restarts` mitigates but does not solve this. Every
> model-selection method below inherits this: a "better" $K$ may simply be a
> better-initialized fit.

> **[A] Label switching.** The likelihood is invariant to the $K!$ relabelings
> of the states. Nothing in the package breaks this symmetry.

---

## Model selection {#sec-ms}

### What we would like

For comparing state counts we want the marginal likelihood

$$
p(Y \mid K) \;=\; \int \sum_{z_{1:T}} p(Y, z_{1:T} \mid \Theta)\; p(\Theta)\,\mathrm{d}\Theta ,
$$

which is intractable twice over: an exponential sum over paths inside a
high-dimensional integral. The package offers three routes, in increasing order
of ambition and of assumptions.

### Cross-validation

Two scoring rules are available: the plug-in predictive (`cross_validate_k`,
below) and the posterior predictive (`posterior_predictive_cv`, @sec-ppcv). The
plug-in rule is the most assumption-light option in the package. Fit on training
data, report $\log p(Y_{\text{test}} \mid \hat\Theta_{\text{train}})$ from the
exact forward pass, and pick the $K$ with the best mean held-out score.

Two regimes:

- **$S > 1$ sequences**: `KFold` over sequences. Held-out sequences are genuinely
  independent of training, so this is a clean predictive estimate.
- **$S = 1$ sequence**: `TimeSeriesSplit`, expanding window.

> **[X] Plug-in predictive.** $\log p(Y_{\text{test}}\mid\hat\Theta)$ is a plug-in
> score, not the posterior predictive $\log p(Y_{\text{test}}\mid Y_{\text{train}})$.
> It ignores parameter uncertainty and so is optimistic, increasingly so for
> large $K$.

> **[A] Test segments restart the chain.** In the single-sequence regime the test
> slice is treated as a fresh sequence beginning at $\pi_0$. The true filtered
> state at the split point is discarded, which penalizes the model for
> information it would actually have had. The bias grows with the persistence of
> the chain.

> **[!] Known defect (open).** `slice_single_sequence` slices transition inputs as
> `x_trans[s-1 : e-1]` for a slice starting at $s$. For the training slice
> ($s=0$) this is correct. For any slice with $s>0$ — i.e. every test slice — the
> transition inputs are **shifted one step early**: the forward pass consumes
> $u_{s-1},\dots$ where it needs $u_{s},\dots$. It does not raise, because the
> length check only runs inside `fit_glmhmm`. Affects input-driven models under
> `TimeSeriesSplit` only.

> **[A] Fold configs.** Folds inherit the full base config (`_replace`), so
> regularization and priors are held fixed across $K$. Because the penalties are
> priors, comparing $K$ at fixed `l2_reg_*` compares models with *different*
> effective prior mass; this is the conventional choice but it is a choice.

#### Posterior-predictive CV {#sec-ppcv}

`posterior_predictive_cv` replaces the plug-in score with the quantity it is
standing in for, using the identity

$$
\log p(Y_{\text{test}} \mid Y_{\text{train}})
= \log Z\big(Y_{\text{train}} \cup Y_{\text{test}}\big) - \log Z\big(Y_{\text{train}}\big),
$$

exact by definition of conditional probability. No posterior over $\Theta$ has to
be represented or sampled — both terms come from the evidence estimators of
@sec-factorized. This removes the two **[X]**/**[A]** items above: parameter
uncertainty is integrated, not plugged in, so the score penalizes extra states
on its own; and in the single-sequence case $Z(\text{union})$ is the marginal
likelihood of the whole prefix, so the latent chain is carried across the split
instead of being restarted at $\pi_0$.

Two incidental benefits. $\log K!$ appears in both terms and **cancels exactly**,
so the label-switching convention is irrelevant here. And both slices used start
at index 0, so the transition-input misalignment that affects mid-sequence
slices cannot arise.

With multiple sequences the union is the whole dataset for every fold, so
$Z(\text{union})$ is computed once and shared; fold scores are correlated
through it and the reported spread reflects only the training-set evidences.

> **[X] Inherits the evidence approximations.** The identity is exact; the two
> terms are not. This is a difference of two independently approximated
> quantities, each large relative to their difference, so the soft-count error
> does not cancel systematically. Check the propagated estimator standard
> deviation against the gaps between candidate $K$ before trusting a ranking.

> **[A] Cost.** $n_{\text{folds}} + 1$ fits *and* evidence evaluations per $K$,
> versus $n_{\text{folds}}$ fits for the plug-in score. The evidence
> computation, not the fitting, dominates.

Measured on 6 sequences of 150 trials from a true $K=3$ model, 3 folds:

| $K$ | plug-in | posterior predictive |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | $-187.49 \pm 5.80$ | $-172.45 \pm 18.37$ |
| **3** | $\mathbf{-177.72 \pm 3.60}$ | $\mathbf{-171.45 \pm 7.63}$ |
| 4 | $-184.51 \pm 6.36$ | $-178.15 \pm 7.21$ |

Both rank $K=3$ first, and every value lies inside $[-2 \cdot 150 \log 2,\ 0]$, the
admissible range for a log predictive density over $2\times150$ binary trials --
a check that the difference behaves like a density rather than an arbitrary
number. The wider fold spread on the right is the cost of differencing two large
estimates.

**Why not sample a posterior directly?** The alternative is a Laplace posterior
at $\hat\Theta$ and a Monte Carlo average of $p(Y_{\text{test}} \mid \Theta_s)$.
Mechanically this is easy -- `compute_log_marginal_likelihood` is a differentiable
`lax.scan`, the free-parameter count is small (9 to 35 for $K = 2,3,4$ here), and
`jax.hessian` handles it. It fails on the model, not the machinery. Measured on a
$K=2,3,4$ sweep: the gradient of the observed-data log posterior at $\hat\Theta$
was $0.57$ at $K=3$ and the Hessian was **indefinite** (smallest eigenvalue
$-0.17$), so there is no Laplace posterior to sample; where $-H$ *was* positive
definite its smallest eigenvalues were $10^{-4}$ and $3\times10^{-5}$. Those
near-flat directions are the singularity discussed in @sec-bic showing up again,
and sampling along them makes the Monte Carlo average diverge upward -- the
inflation was *larger* at $K=4$ than at $K=2$, i.e. it would push the score
toward more states rather than fewer. The identity route avoids the problem by
never needing a posterior.

### BIC {#sec-bic}

$$
\mathrm{BIC} = k \log n - 2\log \hat{L}, \qquad \log \hat Z \approx -\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{BIC}.
$$

Free parameters $k$ are counted honestly against the identifiability
constraints: $D_u K(K{-}1)$ for input-driven transitions or $K(K{-}1)$ for
static, $K-1$ for $\pi_0$, $D(C{-}1)K$ for multinomial, $DMK + K\frac{M(M+1)}{2}$
for Gaussian (weights plus covariances), and the obvious counts elsewhere.

> **[X] Laplace/BIC regularity.** BIC is the $n \to \infty$
> Laplace approximation to $\log p(Y)$ under a regular model with a flat prior.
> **Mixture and hidden Markov models are singular** — the Fisher information is
> rank deficient wherever states coincide or are unoccupied — so the standard BIC
> derivation does not apply, and it typically **over-penalizes** state count.
> This is directly observable here: the smallest eigenvalues of the observed-data
> $-H$ at the fitted optimum came out at $10^{-4}$ ($K=2$) and $3\times10^{-5}$
> ($K=4$), and at $K=3$ the matrix was indefinite outright.

> **[X] MAP substituted for MLE.** $\hat L$ is the penalized (MAP) optimum, not
> the maximum likelihood, and $k$ counts nominal rather than effective degrees of
> freedom — regularization is not discounted.

> **[A] Choice of $n$.** $n$ is taken as the number of *transitions*
> $\sum_i (T_i - 1)$ when transition inputs are present, otherwise the number of
> observations. With Gaussian data the number of samples $\gg$ the number of HMM
> steps, and neither is obviously the right $n$.

### Factorized evidence: the decomposition {#sec-factorized}

This is the ambitious route, shared by both the BQ and SMC implementations. The
derivation has three moves.

**Move 1 — a variational bound over paths.** For any distribution $q(Z)$ over
latent paths, Jensen gives a genuine lower bound

$$
\log p(Y) \;=\; \log \sum_Z p(Y,Z) \;\ge\; \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log p(Y,Z)\big] + \mathbb{H}[q],
$$

where $p(Y,Z) = \int p(Y,Z\mid\Theta)p(\Theta)\,\mathrm{d}\Theta$ is the
*complete-data* marginal likelihood.

**Move 2 — exact factorization given a path.** Conditioned on $Z$, the
complete-data likelihood factorizes across parameter blocks, and if the prior
also factorizes then so does the integral:

$$
p(Y,Z) \;=\; \underbrace{Z_{\pi_0}(Z)}_{\text{Dirichlet–multinomial}}
\;\cdot\; \prod_{i=1}^{K} Z^{\text{trans}}_i(Z)
\;\cdot\; \prod_{k=1}^{K} Z^{\text{glm}}_k(Z) .
$$

Each factor is a low-dimensional integral: one multinomial-logistic evidence per
*source state*, one GLM evidence per *state*. This step is **exact** — it is the
reason the whole scheme is tractable.

**Move 3 — soft counts.** The factors depend on $Z$ only through counts. The
code evaluates each factor at the *expected* counts rather than averaging the
log-factor over the posterior over paths:

$$
\mathbb{E}_q\big[\log Z_\bullet(Z)\big] \;\longrightarrow\; \log Z_\bullet\big(\mathbb{E}_q[\text{counts}]\big),
$$

i.e. hard state indicators are replaced by responsibilities $\gamma_t(k)$ and
hard transition counts by $\xi_t(i,j)$. Putting it together, the reported
quantity is

$$
\boxed{\;\log \hat Z \;=\; \log Z_{\pi_0}(\bar\gamma) \;+\; \sum_i \log Z^{\text{trans}}_i(\bar\xi)
\;+\; \sum_k \log Z^{\text{glm}}_k(\bar\gamma) \;+\; \mathbb{H}[q] \;}
$$

with the entropy computed as the exact identity

$$
\mathbb{H}[q] \;=\; \log p(Y\mid\hat\Theta) \;-\; \mathbb{E}_q\big[\log p(Y,Z\mid\hat\Theta)\big],
$$

which holds when $q$ is the exact posterior $p(Z\mid Y,\hat\Theta)$. This term is
necessarily $\ge 0$ and is a useful correctness check on an implementation.

Now the approximations.

> **[X] Move 3 is not a bound and is the dominant approximation.** Swapping
> $\mathbb{E}[\log Z(\cdot)]$ for $\log Z(\mathbb{E}[\cdot])$ is exact only if
> $q$ is a point mass on one path. The further the state posterior is from
> confident, the larger the error, and its sign is not guaranteed — so the final
> number is **not** a lower bound on $\log p(Y)$ despite Move 1 being one. The
> per-factor "likelihoods" use fractional observation counts and are not the
> likelihood of any dataset.

> **[X] $q$ is plugged in, not optimized.** $q = p(Z\mid Y,\hat\Theta_{\text{MAP}})$
> from a single E-step, rather than a $q$ optimized jointly with a posterior over
> $\Theta$ as in variational Bayes EM. The bound in Move 1 is therefore loose by
> the KL between this $q$ and the true path posterior marginalized over $\Theta$.

> **[A] Prior factorization.** The prior must factorize across the blocks for
> Move 2 to hold. It does: independent Gaussians per weight, independent
> Dirichlets per transition row.

> **[A] $K!$ multiplicity is included.** The factorization expands around a
> single labeling, but the parameter posterior has $K!$ symmetric modes, so
> $\log K!$ is added to recover the full integral. Disable with
> `include_label_switching=False` to compare specific labelled solutions — but
> the setting must then match across BQ and SMC.

> **[X] The expansion point is only approximately the mode.** Both estimators
> assume the fitted parameters maximize the per-factor log-density they
> integrate — for BQ this is essential, since it expands a Laplace approximation
> there. Each M-step *in isolation* returns a stationary point of its own
> objective (verified, gradient $\sim10^{-10}$). But the factors are rebuilt from
> a fresh E-step, and by the staleness noted in @sec-em those are not the
> responsibilities the M-step used: measured transition-factor gradients at
> $\hat\Theta$ were $0.23$ to $2.23$ on a $K=4$ fit. The Laplace expansion is then
> taken slightly off-mode, and the error grows the further EM stops from a fixed
> point. The Gaussian factor does not rely on this at all: see
> @sec-gauss-exact.

### The Gaussian factor is exact {#sec-gauss-exact}

The Gaussian emission factor is a responsibility-weighted multivariate linear
regression, which is conjugate. Rather than approximating it, the package
integrates it analytically over **both** $W$ and $\Sigma$, under

$$
W \mid \Sigma \sim \mathcal{MN}\big(0,\ \Lambda^{-1},\ \Sigma\big), \qquad
\Sigma \sim \mathcal{IW}(\Psi, \nu),
$$

with $\Lambda = \mathrm{diag}(\rho)$, $\rho_0 = 1/\texttt{prior\_var\_bias\_emit}$
and $\rho_{d>0} = \texttt{l2\_reg\_gauss}$. Writing
$S_{xx} = X^\top\!\mathrm{diag}(w)X + \Lambda$, $S_{xy} = X^\top\!\mathrm{diag}(w)Y$,
$S_{yy} = Y^\top\!\mathrm{diag}(w)Y$, $n = \sum_s w_s$ and
$\Psi_N = \Psi + S_{yy} - S_{xy}^\top S_{xx}^{-1} S_{xy}$:

$$
\log Z = -\frac{nM}{2}\log\pi
+ \frac{M}{2}\big(\log|\Lambda| - \log|S_{xx}|\big)
+ \frac{\nu}{2}\log|\Psi| - \frac{\nu + n}{2}\log|\Psi_N|
+ \log\Gamma_M\!\Big(\frac{\nu+n}{2}\Big) - \log\Gamma_M\!\Big(\frac{\nu}{2}\Big).
$$

The per-sample weights $w_s$ are the state responsibilities, carrying the
$1/(L_t M)$ factor of @sec-gauss-norm when the rescaling is active — the
rescaling remains a per-sample weight, so the conjugate algebra is unaffected.

Three consequences. The matrix-normal prior (column covariance $\Sigma$) is
**not** an arbitrary choice: it is exactly the prior implied by the closed-form
Gaussian M-step, whose normal equations are the stationarity condition of this
density for any $\Sigma$. $\Sigma$ is integrated rather than plugged in, so the
$K\,M(M{+}1)/2$ covariance parameters now carry an Occam penalty. And because
this factor is exact, BQ and SMC return **identical** values for Gaussian-only
models.

> **[A] Inverse-Wishart hyperparameters.** Defaults are $\nu = M+2$, the smallest
> integer degrees of freedom for which $\mathbb{E}[\Sigma] = \Psi/(\nu - M - 1)$
> exists, and $\Psi = \texttt{iw\_scale\_gauss}\cdot I$ with
> `iw_scale_gauss = 1.0`. **$\Psi$ carries the units of $y_{\text{gauss}}$
> squared**: the default assumes roughly standardised Gaussian data, and should
> be set to about the expected residual variance otherwise. The evidence is
> sensitive to this choice, as it is to any prior on a parameter being
> integrated.

### Bayesian quadrature estimator

For each factor with log-density $f(\vartheta)$ and mode $\hat\vartheta$
(`run_bq_tinygp`):

1. **Laplace.** $H = \nabla^2 f(\hat\vartheta)$, regularized to $H - 10^{-4}I$,
   giving $\Sigma_L = (-H + 10^{-4}I)^{-1}$ and
   $\log Z_{\text{Lap}} = f(\hat\vartheta) + \tfrac{d}{2}\log 2\pi - \tfrac12\log\det(-H_{\text{reg}})$.
2. **Whiten and sample.** Draw $n$ samples from $q = \mathcal{N}(\hat\vartheta, \Sigma_L)$
   and form the ratios $r(\vartheta) = \exp\big(f(\vartheta) - \log q(\vartheta) - \log Z_{\text{Lap}}\big)$,
   so that $\mathbb{E}_q[r] = Z / Z_{\text{Lap}}$.
3. **Quadrature.** Rather than the Monte Carlo mean, fit a GP to $r - \bar r$ in
   whitened coordinates and integrate the GP posterior mean against
   $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ analytically, giving $\bar r + z^\top K^{-1}(r - \bar r)$
   with $z_i = \int k(\cdot, x_i)\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)$.
4. **Report** $\log Z_{\text{Lap}} + \log(\text{integral})$, plus a delta-method
   variance $\mathrm{Var}[\log Z] \approx \mathrm{Var}[\hat I]/\hat I^2$.

> **[X] Laplace as the base measure.** Step 1 assumes the factor posterior is
> unimodal and well approximated by a Gaussian at the mode; the GP in step 3 only
> corrects the *residual*. If the Laplace fit is poor the importance ratios have
> heavy tails and the correction is unreliable.

> **[X] GP hyperparameters are fitted, on a subset.** The `ExpSquared`
> lengthscale and variance are obtained by maximizing the GP marginal likelihood
> (`fit_gp_hyperparameters`) rather than left at $1.0$. Fitting uses a random
> subset of at most 512 points, since each objective evaluation costs a dense
> Cholesky. Disable with `tune_gp_hyperparameters=False`.
>
> Fitted lengthscales are typically 3–10 in whitened coordinates, well above the
> old default of 1. That makes the Gram matrix strongly correlated, so the
> Cholesky jitter is scaled to the kernel variance and escalated until the
> factorization is finite (`stable_cholesky`) — JAX returns NaN rather than
> raising, so this has to be checked explicitly. If conditioning fails anyway,
> the factor degrades to the plain Monte Carlo mean and warns. Empirically the
> tuned and untuned estimates agree to $\sim 0.005$ nats when the Laplace fit is
> good, because a good fit leaves almost no residual for the GP to correct; the
> tuning matters where the fit is poor.

> **[X] Ratio sanitization.** Non-finite ratios must still be made finite
> (`nan_to_num`, $+\infty \mapsto 10^{6}$), but the fraction sanitized is now
> tracked and a `RuntimeWarning` is raised above 1%. A warning here means the
> Laplace base measure is a poor fit and the factor's value should not be
> trusted.

> **[A] Cost.** $n = \mathrm{clip}(500 d,\ 2000,\ 8000)$ samples by default, then
> a dense $n \times n$ Cholesky: $O(n^2)$ memory and $O(n^3)$ time **per factor
> per state**. The ceiling (`max_samples`) bounds what was previously unbounded
> growth in $d$; raising it improves quadrature accuracy at cubic cost.

### Sequential Monte Carlo estimator

Adaptive tempered SMC (`blackjax`) per factor: a particle population is
transported along $p_\lambda(\vartheta) \propto p(\vartheta)\,
p(\text{data}\mid\vartheta)^\lambda$ from $\lambda=0$ to $\lambda=1$, with the
temperature ladder chosen adaptively to hold ESS at 50%, and NUTS or HMC
rejuvenation between stages. The evidence is the telescoping product of
normalizing-constant increments,
$\log Z = \sum_m \log \mathbb{E}_{m-1}\big[\,\ell^{\lambda_m - \lambda_{m-1}}\big]$.

> **[A] Particles are drawn from the prior.** The estimator's validity rests on
> the $\lambda=0$ population being prior-distributed. Every prior in the module
> is a product of independent zero-mean Gaussians, so `run_smc_factor` samples it
> exactly via `diagonal_gaussian_prior_sampler` — no MCMC and no bias. This costs
> tempering steps relative to starting at the MAP, which is the honest price of a
> valid normalizing constant.

> **[X] Fixed MCMC tuning.** Step size $0.5/\sqrt{d}$ and identity inverse mass
> matrix, with no adaptation. Defaults are 150 particles and 10 rejuvenation
> steps. If the tempering path is long, rejuvenation quality is what limits
> accuracy.

> **[A] Monte Carlo error.** A single call returns a point estimate.
> `compute_factorized_evidence_smc_replicated` runs independent replicates and
> reports mean and standard deviation — the number that differences in log
> evidence between models must be compared against.

### Which to trust

| | CV (plug-in) | CV (posterior pred.) | BIC | BQ / SMC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Estimates | $\log p(Y_{\text{test}} \mid \hat\Theta)$ | $\log p(Y_{\text{test}} \mid Y_{\text{train}})$ | $\log p(Y)$, asymptotically | $\log p(Y)$, variationally |
| Path sum | exact | soft-count **[X]** | exact | soft-count **[X]** |
| Parameter integral | none | via the evidence | Laplace, $n\to\infty$ | BQ: Laplace+GP / SMC: tempered / Gaussian: exact |
| Penalises extra states | **no** | yes | yes | yes |
| Valid for singular models | yes | partly | **no** | partly |
| Cost | folds $\times$ restarts fits | $(\text{folds}{+}1)\times$ (fit + evidence) | negligible | dominant |
| Open defects | temporal-split shift | — | — | — |

BQ and SMC now integrate the same model with the same priors, so they should
agree to within Monte Carlo error. Measured on a 3-state Bernoulli model with
input-driven transitions: BQ $-155.17$, SMC $-155.41 \pm 0.20$ over three
replicates — a $0.24$ nat difference against a $0.20$ nat replicate spread. On
Gaussian-only models they agree to $0.000$ nats, since every factor is then
either closed-form conjugate or a Dirichlet–multinomial. **A disagreement much
larger than the SMC replicate spread is a signal that one of the estimators is
struggling, not a modelling result.**

**Recommendation.** Plug-in CV over independent sequences is the most
assumption-light option and sidesteps the soft-count substitution entirely — but
it does not penalise extra states, and that is not a theoretical quibble.
`tests/test_model_selection_bernoulli_input_driven.py` scores all three methods on
one dataset generated from a true $K=3$ model (10 sequences of 250 trials, both
transitions and emissions input-driven), higher being better throughout:

| $K$ | CV test LL | implied $\log Z$ ($-\mathrm{BIC}/2$) | BQ $\log Z$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | $-312.70$ | $-1580.34$ | $-1570.92$ |
| **3** | $-302.89$ | $\mathbf{-1559.06}$ | $\mathbf{-1534.89}$ |
| 4 | $\mathbf{-300.93}$ | $-1619.00$ | $-1567.74$ |

BIC and BQ recover $K=3$ by $21.3$ and $32.9$ nats respectively. Plug-in CV picks
$K=4$ — but by $1.96$ nats against its own fold-to-fold spread of $\pm 8$ to
$10$, so read it as indifference to the extra state rather than confidence in it,
which is exactly what a score with no complexity penalty should do.

So: use plug-in CV to check that a model predicts held-out data at all, and use
the evidence — directly, or differenced through `posterior_predictive_cv` — to
choose $K$. The factorized evidence earns its cost when sequences are few and
long, where CV has little to hold out. Its remaining error is dominated by Move 3,
not by the quadrature or the sampler, so effort spent tuning BQ or SMC settings
buys less than effort spent making the state posterior confident.

## What has been checked numerically {#sec-verified}

Claims of exactness above are not asserted from inspection. The following were
checked against independent references; numbers are the observed agreement.

| Claim | Reference used | Agreement |
|---|---|---|
| $\sum_t c_t = \log p(Y)$; $\gamma$, $\xi$ correct | exhaustive enumeration of all $K^T$ paths ($K{=}3$, $T{=}7$, time-varying $A_t$) | $\sim10^{-16}$ |
| $\sum_j \xi_t(i,j) = \gamma_t(i)$, $\sum_i \xi_t(i,j) = \gamma_{t+1}(j)$ | same | $\sim10^{-16}$ |
| Viterbi path and log-probability | exhaustive argmax over all paths | exact |
| All five emission log-densities | `scipy.stats` | $\sim10^{-15}$ |
| $A_t[i,j] = \mathrm{softmax}_j(u_t\cdot\theta)$ | direct construction | $\sim10^{-16}$ |
| Each M-step objective $= -\sum_n \gamma_{nk}\log p + \text{penalty}$ | emission functions | exact (Bern, multinom); $\sim10^{-7}$ (NegBin, Gamma — the epsilon) |
| M-step returns a stationary point | autodiff gradient of the exact objective | $\sim10^{-10}$; $\sim10^{-4}$ for NegBin/Gamma |
| Gaussian $W$, $\Sigma$ closed forms | direct weighted ridge / weighted covariance | $\sim10^{-17}$ |
| $\pi_0$ update is the Dirichlet MAP | direct computation | $\sim10^{-10}$ |
| MAP-EM ascends $\mathcal{F}$ | 40 iterations of a real fit | min step $+6.8\times10^{-3}$ |
| Gaussian factor closed form (@sec-gauss-exact) | 2-D numerical quadrature ($D{=}M{=}1$) | $2.8\times10^{-8}$ |
| same, $M{=}2$ | $2\times10^5$ prior Monte Carlo draws | $0.047$ nats |
| $\log\Gamma_M$ | `scipy.special.multigammaln` | $<10^{-10}$ |
| Dirichlet–multinomial static transition evidence | analytic $\log B(\alpha+n)-\log B(\alpha)$ | exact to 2 dp |
| BQ and SMC agree | 3-state Bernoulli, input-driven | $0.24$ nats vs SMC replicate sd $0.20$ |
| same, Gaussian-only | — | $0.000$ nats (both exact there) |
| $\log K!$ term | $\log 3! = 1.7918$ | $1.7917$ |
| Posterior-predictive CV in range | $[-2T\log 2,\ 0]$ bound | satisfied at all $K$ |

`tests/test_model_selection_bernoulli_input_driven.py` exercises CV, BIC and BQ
together on one dataset with input-driven transitions *and* emissions.

## Summary of assumptions and approximations {#sec-summary}

**Model**

| | Item |
|---|---|
| **[A]** | Transition inputs aligned to $t \to t+1$, length $T-1$ |
| **[A]** | Emission families conditionally independent given the state |
| **[A]** | Column 0 of every design matrix is the bias |
| **[A]** | Gaussian segments contiguous, ordered, tiling from index 0 |
| **[A]** | Sequences mutually independent |
| **[A]** | Log-link means clipped ($\le e^{20}$; Gamma also $\ge e^{-10}$) |
| **[X]** | Gaussian pseudo-likelihood rescaling by $1/(L_t M)$ |

**Inference and learning**

| | Item |
|---|---|
| — | Forward–backward, posteriors and Viterbi are **exact** (verified) |
| — | Every M-step optimises exactly the likelihood the E-step scores (verified) |
| **[X]** | MAP not MLE; L2 penalties are Gaussian priors |
| **[X]** | Generalized EM: M-steps are iterative to `tol`, not exact |
| **[X]** | Returned parameters lag their own responsibilities by one M-step |
| **[X]** | Dispersion $\pm 10^{-6}$ epsilon; Gamma shape/rate mixed |
| **[A]** | Local optima; label switching unbroken |

**Model selection**

| | Item |
|---|---|
| **[X]** | CV (plug-in): ignores parameter uncertainty, no complexity penalty |
| **[A]** | CV (plug-in): temporal test slices restart from $\pi_0$ |
| **[!]** | CV (plug-in): transition inputs shifted one step in temporal test slices |
| — | CV (posterior predictive): identity is **exact**; avoids all three above |
| **[X]** | CV (posterior predictive): inherits the evidence approximations |
| **[X]** | BIC: regularity assumption invalid for singular models |
| **[X]** | BIC: MAP substituted for MLE, nominal d.o.f. |
| **[A]** | BIC: ambiguous choice of $n$ |
| — | Factorization given a path is **exact** |
| — | Gaussian factor is **exact** (matrix-normal / inverse-Wishart conjugacy) |
| **[X]** | Soft-count substitution — dominant error, not a bound |
| **[X]** | $q(Z)$ plugged in from one E-step, not optimized |
| **[A]** | Inverse-Wishart hyperparameters carry the units of $y_{\text{gauss}}$ |
| **[A]** | $\log K!$ multiplicity included by default |
| **[X]** | Laplace expansion point is only approximately the mode |
| **[X]** | BQ: Laplace base measure; GP fitted on a $\le512$-point subset |
| **[X]** | BQ: ratio sanitization and GP conditioning, both warned about |
| **[X]** | SMC: fixed MCMC tuning; MC error needs replicates |

Items marked **[!]** are defects rather than design choices. The only one
outstanding is the transition-input shift in temporal CV splits; every
**[!]** item in the factorized estimators has been resolved.
